title: Samuel Ajayi Crowther
hook: freed from a slave ship as a boy, he becomes the first African Anglican bishop (1864)

segments.voice: Yesterday: missions and empire, and local Christians who led, like Ramabai. Your line was the gospel is not an empire.

A Yoruba boy named Ajayi is taken in a raid on his town, in what is now Nigeria. He is sold, and sold again, and put in chains on a slave ship bound across the Atlantic. Before the ship gets far, a British navy ship stops it. The captives are brought to Sierra Leone and set free. The boy who walks off that deck has lost his home and has no word of his family. Years later, he will walk into a cathedral in England and come out a bishop. Today: Samuel Ajayi Crowther.
screen: `A YORUBA BOY, TAKEN IN A RAID.`

segments.voice: In Sierra Leone the boy went to a mission school, learned to read quickly, and was baptized, taking the name Samuel Crowther. He kept Ajayi too. He studied, taught, and was ordained a priest. Then he became what the missions badly needed: a translator. He worked on putting the Bible into Yoruba, his own first language, and helped with grammars and word lists for other languages along the Niger River. He wanted people to hear the gospel in the words their mothers used. Tradition says that on one trip home he found his own mother, years after the raid, and that she too was later baptized. Then he was made a bishop, to lead the church's mission on the Niger, and Anglicans remember him as their first African bishop. The story doesn't end clean. In his old age, younger European missionaries criticized his work and pushed his African clergy aside, and he was sidelined. Some who tell his story see in it the same arrogance named yesterday. Hold all of it. The thread through his life is in words Jesus chose from Isaiah, reading in the synagogue at Nazareth, in the King James Bible: "he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives." Crowther had been a captive. He was delivered, and he spent his life carrying the word that freed him back toward his own people. Paul wrote: "Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free." For Crowther, being freed wasn't the end of the story. It was a job.

Bring to mind Nigeria, a country you may know only from headlines: its markets, its churches and mosques, its children walking to school this morning. Picture a Yoruba hymn sung somewhere right now, in a language Crowther helped put on paper. If you pray, pray for Nigeria's people, for peace and daily bread; if you don't, let your attention rest there kindly.
Crowther. Freed from a slave ship as a boy, he became a translator of the Bible into Yoruba and the first African Anglican bishop on the Niger.
Your line: freed to free. What once set you free can be handed on. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Anglicans in Nigeria and beyond remember Crowther in their calendars and prayers, and Yoruba-speaking Christians still read and sing from the Bible and hymns in their own language.

chat.says: How did a boy taken on a slave ship end up a bishop?
options: He was freed, schooled, translated the Bible into Yoruba, and was made bishop on the Niger.
He escaped to England as a boy and trained there to become a London bishop.
He was born free in Sierra Leone and never saw a slave ship himself.
chat.meaning: Freed in Sierra Leone, Crowther studied, was ordained, translated the Bible into Yoruba, and was made a bishop for the Niger mission.

Yoruba.meaning: a people and language of what is now Nigeria

Niger River.meaning: the West African river where he led the church's mission

Nazareth.meaning: the town where Jesus read from Isaiah in the synagogue

Ajayi.meaning: his Yoruba name, which he kept after baptism
